headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can read/write application-defined files and uses stdin/stdout; Agent B consumes files like AGENTS.md/README.md and uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. That creates a plausible instruction-injection path through shared content, though the exact bridge is not fully documented. Uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or repo files, injected instructions in those files can influence B.
IF B parses AGENTS.md or README.md as operational guidance, attacker-authored text can steer tool use.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic instruction parsing for shared files.
Require provenance tags on file-fed instructions.
Review AGENTS.md/README.md before each run.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance checks.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches graph state and model-provider API keys, while B touches session history, project code, and provider authentication data. Both have broad network egress and file access, so a shared workspace or shared credentials could leak sensitive material between them. The profiles do not prove isolation, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF A and B share a filesystem or checkpointer-backed workspace, B may read A's graph state.
IF either agent is configured with the same provider credentials, session history or auth data can cross-contaminate outputs.
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers.
Rotate and scope provider API keys per agent.
Keep checkpointer stores isolated.
Audit shared directories for secrets.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret vaulting.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; B can also spawn subprocesses and uses full-permissions mode with runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. If they share a writable directory or mutable config, concurrent writes can race and corrupt state. Because the profiles do not show locking, the conflict pathway is plausible in default orchestration.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same writable directory, file clobbering or config corruption can occur.
IF B's hooks mutate files while A is running subprocesses, race conditions can break execution state.
mitigations: Assign disjoint working directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Disable full-permissions mode for B.
Run one agent at a time on shared assets.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a low-level orchestration framework that can emit graph state, and B is a customer-support agent with broad egress and runtime-injected tools. If B treats A's outputs as authoritative, an error in A can cascade into external actions or user-facing responses. No verification step is documented, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated state or summaries without verification, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF B is allowed to send messages or call external APIs based on A's output, the error can become user-visible.
mitigations: Add a human review step for A outputs.
Require schema validation before B consumes A state.
Log and diff A-to-B handoffs.
Limit B to read-only use of A outputs.
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles model-provider API keys and graph state; B handles provider auth prompts, session history, project code, and telemetry. Both have broad egress and no documented residency or retention controls, so a retention or logging mismatch is plausible. The profiles do not show a specific regulated data class, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into B's session history or telemetry, retention policy mismatch becomes a compliance issue.
IF A's graph state contains customer data and B uploads it to third-party services, residency or logging obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared sessions.
Disable or minimize telemetry.
Review retention settings for both agents.
Separate auth prompts from customer data.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls.
